common_name: Fun and Games Red Rover Heucherella

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants out after the soil has warmed in spring, or in early fall, into humus-rich soil in part shade.

directions: Red Rover is a Fun and Games series heucherella with heavily lobed, finger-like leaves that open coppery red with a dark burgundy center before easing to olive green as summer heat arrives. Wiry stems carry creamy white bottlebrush flowers from late spring into fall, drawing bees over a long season. Plant in evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, where its low, wide-spreading habit works well as edging or a groundcover drift. Divide congested clumps in spring every few years to keep the foliage color fresh.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall into poor-to-average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; it is unfussy about soil fertility.

directions: Ru-Bee Wren opens new growth in a brilliant crimson flush each spring before settling into deep green through summer, a stronger color show than the species typically offers. Clusters of nectar-rich yellow flowers appear in late June and draw butterflies, followed by dry capsules that persist into winter and bring in seed-eating birds. It tolerates rocky, nutrient-poor soil and spreads gradually by suckering to knit together a colony on slopes or woodland edges. Little pruning is needed beyond removing old canes occasionally to refresh the planting.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil; a second seedling or cultivar is needed nearby for cross-pollination and nut set.

directions: This selection pairs the reliable fall nut crop of native American hazelnut with heart-shaped foliage that holds a deep wine-purple color all season before shifting to burgundy and bronze in autumn. It tolerates part shade better than most nut shrubs, though heavier shade reduces nut production, and it suckers over time into a multi-stemmed thicket useful as an informal screen. Harvest nuts as husks begin to brown and split in September and October, checking often since squirrels compete for the crop. Plant with a second genetically distinct hazelnut nearby, since it is self-incompatible and needs cross-pollination to bear well.

planting.note: Set out plugs or divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade, spacing closely for faster coverage.

directions: Silver Gem is a trailing selection of the southeastern native creeping violet, its small rounded leaves heavily brushed with silver variegation that makes the mat ornamentally interesting even between bloom cycles. Pale lavender flowers open in early spring and continue sporadically through the growing season rather than concentrating into one flush. Stems root as they spread along the soil surface, slowly filling in bare ground beneath shrubs and trees without becoming aggressive. Once established it tolerates considerable drought, making it a low-care option for dry shade where many groundcovers struggle.

planting.note: Press small divisions or stem cuttings into moist, well-drained soil in part to full shade; rooted pieces establish quickly without special care.

directions: Larinem Park is a named selection of the only native eastern sedum genuinely adapted to shade, forming low whorls of small fleshy green leaves that stay evergreen in milder winters. Starry white flowers rise just above the foliage for several weeks in spring and draw small native bees and butterflies. Unlike sun-loving stonecrops, it performs best tucked beneath shrubs or trees in soil that drains well but is not bone dry, making it useful on shaded rocky slopes where turf and most other groundcovers fail. Deer generally leave it alone, and established mats need no routine maintenance beyond the occasional edge trim.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in gritty, very well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; sharp drainage matters more than light level for this selection.

directions: Short and Sweet is a compact selection of wild pink bred for a tidy, low profile well suited to small beds, rock gardens, and containers where the straight species can sprawl. Deep pink, five-petaled flowers open on sticky-stemmed rosettes in late spring and can continue for weeks on end, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds to the nectar-rich blooms. Flowering is heaviest with at least a few hours of direct sun, though the plant survives in fuller shade with a lighter bloom display. It demands sharp drainage above all else and will quickly decline in heavy or poorly drained soil, so a gravelly or sandy site suits it best.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; it tolerates coastal wind and light salt spray once rooted in.

directions: Bobee grows into a dense, globe-shaped mound of deep green, strongly aromatic foliage that releases its bayberry scent readily when brushed or crushed. Female plants carry waxy gray berries through fall and winter that persist on the stems as an important food source for overwintering songbirds. It is tough and adaptable, shrugging off drought, sandy infertile soil, and the wind and salt exposure typical of coastal plantings. Give it room to reach its full rounded spread, since it needs little pruning beyond the occasional removal of wayward stems to keep the globe shape tidy.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; a male plant nearby improves berry set on this female selection.

directions: Brave Athena is a female northern bayberry selection with densely held, deep green leaves that turn burgundy in autumn before gray, waxy berries take over as the main seasonal attraction. The berries cling through the cold months and are a reliable late-winter food source for returning songbirds when little else is available. It handles salt spray, wind, and dry sandy soil without complaint, making it a dependable choice for coastal gardens and exposed sites. Pair it with a male bayberry nearby to ensure dependable fruit set, since this is a female clone that needs pollen from a separate plant.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in light to partial shade; the tall stems benefit from the support of nearby shrubs as they lengthen.

directions: Fusion is a selection of the tall Chinese climbing Solomon's seal, sending up sturdy stalks lined with whorled leaves that can reach a full five feet by season's end, taller than most garden Solomon's seals. Like its relatives it goes fully dormant in winter, dying back to a thick underground rhizome before pushing up fresh growth each spring once the soil warms. Grow it in rich, evenly moist woodland soil in dappled shade, where the climbing stems look best leaning against a shrub or low support rather than standing unsupported. Established clumps can be divided in fall every few years to control spread or to start new plantings elsewhere in the shade garden.
